summary.text: Letting \(c_0=4,c_1=16,c_2=63\) and \(c_{n+3}=4c_{n+2}-c_n\), the proof studies the defect \(E_n=c_{n+1}^2-c_{n+2}c_n\), derives \(E_{n+3}=4E_{n+1}+E_n\), and inductively proves \(1\le E_n\le c_n\). Hence \(\lceil c_{n+1}^2/c_n\rceil-1=c_{n+2}\), so induction identifies the original nonlinear sequence with \(c_n\), whose recurrence gives the claimed generating function.

full_proof.text:
Let \((b_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the sequence given by the original definition. Thus
\[
b_0=4,\qquad b_1=16,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge 0\), \(b_{n+2}\) is the greatest integer satisfying
\[
\frac{b_{n+2}}{b_{n+1}}<\frac{b_{n+1}}{b_n}.
\]
All terms that occur below are positive. Multiplying the displayed inequality by the positive number \(b_{n+1}b_n\), the condition on an integer \(q=b_{n+2}\) becomes
\[
q<\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}.
\]
For any real number \(r\), the greatest integer strictly smaller than \(r\) is \(\lceil r\rceil-1\), whether or not \(r\) itself is an integer. Hence the original rule is equivalently
\[
 b_{n+2}=\left\lceil\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}\right\rceil-1. \tag{1}
\]
We prove that this nonlinear recurrence produces the sequence whose generating function is
\[
\frac{4-x^2}{1-4x+x^3}.
\]

Define an auxiliary sequence \((c_n)_{n\ge0}\) by
\[
c_0=4,\qquad c_1=16,\qquad c_2=63,
\]
and
\[
c_{n+3}=4c_{n+2}-c_n\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{2}
\]
The subtraction in (2) causes no difficulty; we will in fact show that all the relevant quantities are positive and that the equivalent additive identity
\[
c_{n+3}+c_n=4c_{n+2} \tag{3}
\]
holds.

First, \((c_n)\) is nondecreasing. The first two comparisons are
\[
4=c_0\le c_1=16\le c_2=63.
\]
Suppose inductively that all earlier consecutive comparisons have been proved, and consider the comparison \(c_{m+2}\le c_{m+3}\). We then have \(c_m\le c_{m+2}\), and (2) gives
\[
c_{m+3}=4c_{m+2}-c_m\ge 4c_{m+2}-c_{m+2}=3c_{m+2}\ge c_{m+2}.
\]
Thus \(c_n\le c_{n+1}\) for every \(n\). In particular,
\[
c_n\ge c_0=4>0 \tag{4}
\]
for all \(n\). Moreover, since \(c_n\le c_{n+2}\le 4c_{n+2}\), equation (2) may indeed be rearranged without truncated-subtraction issues to give (3).

The key point is to control how far the quotient \(c_{n+1}^2/c_n\) lies above the integer \(c_{n+2}\). Define a second sequence \((E_n)_{n\ge0}\) by
\[
E_0=4,\qquad E_1=1,\qquad E_2=16,
\]
and
\[
E_{n+3}=4E_{n+1}+E_n\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{5}
\]
We will prove the exact identity
\[
c_{n+1}^2=c_{n+2}c_n+E_n \qquad(n\ge0). \tag{6}
\]

To see why (5) is the correct recurrence, work temporarily with integer differences
\[
D_n=c_{n+1}^2-c_{n+2}c_n.
\]
Direct calculation gives
\[
D_0=16^2-63\cdot4=256-252=4.
\]
Using (2),
\[
c_3=4c_2-c_0=4\cdot63-4=248,
\]
so
\[
D_1=63^2-248\cdot16=3969-3968=1.
\]
Also
\[
c_4=4c_3-c_1=4\cdot248-16=976,
\]
and hence
\[
D_2=248^2-976\cdot63=61504-61488=16.
\]
Thus \(D_0,D_1,D_2\) agree with \(E_0,E_1,E_2\).

We next verify that \(D_n\) obeys the same recurrence as \(E_n\). For readability, fix \(m\ge0\). From (3),
\[
c_{m+3}=4c_{m+2}-c_m,
\quad
c_{m+4}=4c_{m+3}-c_{m+1},
\quad
c_{m+5}=4c_{m+4}-c_{m+2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_{m+3}
 &=c_{m+4}^2-c_{m+5}c_{m+3}\\
 &=c_{m+4}^2-(4c_{m+4}-c_{m+2})c_{m+3}\\
 &=c_{m+4}(c_{m+4}-4c_{m+3})+c_{m+2}c_{m+3}\\
 &=-c_{m+1}c_{m+4}+c_{m+2}c_{m+3}.
\end{aligned}
\]
On the other hand,
\[
\begin{aligned}
4D_{m+1}+D_m
 &=4(c_{m+2}^2-c_{m+3}c_{m+1})
   +(c_{m+1}^2-c_{m+2}c_m)\\
 &=c_{m+1}^2-4c_{m+3}c_{m+1}
   +c_{m+2}(4c_{m+2}-c_m)\\
 &=c_{m+1}^2-4c_{m+3}c_{m+1}+c_{m+2}c_{m+3}\\
 &=-c_{m+1}(4c_{m+3}-c_{m+1})+c_{m+2}c_{m+3}\\
 &=-c_{m+1}c_{m+4}+c_{m+2}c_{m+3}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
D_{m+3}=4D_{m+1}+D_m.
\]
The initial values and strong induction now show that \(D_n=E_n\) for every \(n\), proving (6).

We need two bounds on the defect:
\[
1\le E_n\le c_n \qquad(n\ge0). \tag{7}
\]
The lower bound is immediate from (5). It holds for the initial values \(E_0=4,E_1=1,E_2=16\); and if it holds at the earlier indices \(m\) and \(m+1\), then
\[
E_{m+3}=4E_{m+1}+E_m\ge4\cdot1+1\ge1.
\]
Thus every \(E_n\) is positive.

For the upper bound, first compute the additional initial values
\[
E_3=4E_1+E_0=8,
\qquad
E_4=4E_2+E_1=65.
\]
Together with
\[
(c_0,c_1,c_2,c_3,c_4)=(4,16,63,248,976),
\]
these give
\[
E_j\le c_j\qquad(0\le j\le4).
\]
Now suppose, by strong induction, that the upper bound has been proved at all indices below \(m+5\). Equation (5) gives
\[
E_{m+5}=4E_{m+3}+E_{m+2}
       \le4c_{m+3}+c_{m+2}. \tag{8}
\]
It remains to compare the right side with \(c_{m+5}\).

Set, just for this comparison,
\[
e=c_{m+3},\qquad d=c_{m+2},\qquad f=c_{m+4},\qquad b=c_{m+1},\qquad g=c_{m+5}.
\]
Monotonicity gives \(b\le e\) and \(d\le e\). From (3),
\[
f+b=4e.
\]
Because \(b+d\le2e\le3e\), we have
\[
e+d+b\le4e=f+b,
\]
and cancellation of \(b\) yields
\[
f\ge e+d.
\]
Hence
\[
4f\ge4e+4d\ge4e+2d.
\]
Using (3) once more, now in the form \(g+d=4f\), we obtain
\[
g+d\ge4e+2d,
\]
so
\[
g\ge4e+d.
\]
In the original notation this is
\[
c_{m+5}\ge4c_{m+3}+c_{m+2}.
\]
Combining this with (8) proves \(E_{m+5}\le c_{m+5}\), completing the induction and establishing (7).

We can now evaluate the ceiling in (1) exactly when the preceding terms are terms of \((c_n)\). By (6),
\[
\frac{c_{m+1}^2}{c_m}
 =c_{m+2}+\frac{E_m}{c_m}.
\]
The bounds (7) and positivity (4) show
\[
0<\frac{E_m}{c_m}\le1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\left\lceil\frac{c_{m+1}^2}{c_m}\right\rceil=c_{m+2}+1, \tag{9}
\]
including the endpoint case \(E_m=c_m\). Equivalently, in integer-division form, (6) gives
\[
c_{m+1}^2+c_m-1
 =c_m(c_{m+2}+1)+(E_m-1),
\]
and \(0\le E_m-1<c_m\); division by \(c_m\) therefore has quotient \(c_{m+2}+1\). This is precisely the standard formula
\(
\lceil u/v\rceil=(u+v-1)\mathbin{/}v
\)
for positive integers \(u,v\).

We now prove by strong induction that
\[
b_n=c_n\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{10}
\]
For \(n=0,1\), this follows from the common initial values. Suppose (10) holds through the indices needed to compute \(b_{m+2}\); in particular,
\[
b_m=c_m,
\qquad
b_{m+1}=c_{m+1}.
\]
Then the original recurrence (1), followed by (9), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{m+2}
 &=\left\lceil\frac{b_{m+1}^2}{b_m}\right\rceil-1\\
 &=\left\lceil\frac{c_{m+1}^2}{c_m}\right\rceil-1\\
 &=(c_{m+2}+1)-1=c_{m+2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This completes the induction. In particular, the original-definition sequence begins
\[
4,16,63,248,976,3841,\ldots
\]
and, because it equals \((c_n)\), satisfies
\[
b_0=4,\qquad b_1=16,\qquad b_2=63,
\]
and for every \(n\ge3\),
\[
b_n=4b_{n-1}-b_{n-3}. \tag{11}
\]
Equivalently, to avoid subtraction,
\[
b_n+b_{n-3}=4b_{n-1}.
\]
This proves the stated recurrence form of the conjecture, including the separate cases \(n=0,1,2\).

Finally, let
\[
G(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}b_nx^n
\]
be the ordinary generating function, interpreted as a formal power series. The coefficient of \(x^n\) in
\[
(1-4x+x^3)G(x)
\]
is \(b_n-4b_{n-1}+b_{n-3}\), with terms having negative indices omitted. For \(n\ge3\), this coefficient is zero by (11). The first three coefficients are
\[
\begin{aligned}
[x^0]&: b_0=4,\\
[x^1]&: b_1-4b_0=16-16=0,\\
[x^2]&: b_2-4b_1=63-64=-1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
(1-4x+x^3)G(x)=4-x^2,
\]
and consequently
\[
\boxed{G(x)=\frac{4-x^2}{1-4x+x^3}}.
\]
Hence the sequence produced by the original extremal consecutive-ratio definition has exactly the conjectured generating function.
